newsitem.title: USA: Judge in Reynolds suit sees extended trial.
newsitem.headline: Judge in Reynolds suit sees extended trial.

text.p: The judge hearing a wrongful death suit against R.J. Reynolds indicated on Thursday that he thought the case could stretch to four weeks instead of the two to three weeks, as originally expected.
Judge Bernard Nachman said he wanted the attorneys to complete their cases by the week of April 28. The plaintiff's attorneys said they expected to rest their case in the middle of next week.

Also on Thursday, attorneys for plaintiff Dana Raulerson sought to introduce as evidence an April 1974 memo from Leonard Zahn, a publicist for the tobacco industry-funded Council for Tobacco Research.

In the letter sent to Henry Ramm, president of the Council for Tobacco Research, Zahn discussed how he had managed to cancel a press conference at which a scientist who had a contract from the council had intended to talk about research showing that inhaling cigarette smoke had produced cancerous changes in hamsters.
"I doubt if you... will want to retain this note," the postscript of the letter said.
Reynolds attorney Jim Johnson argued that there was no way to know whether the document was authentic and that it was not relevant to the case because it did not involve Reynolds executives.
Nachman said the plaintiffs would have to connect the document to Reynolds before he would introduce it. Ron Motley, co-counsel for the plaintiffs, said he would do so on Friday.

Earlier Thursday, the plaintiffs had introduced as evidence a 1962 internal company document in which a Reynolds researcher said there was "overwhelming" evidence of the health hazards of cigarette smoking.
Raulerson has sued Reynolds on behalf of her sister, Jean Connor who smoked heavily and died at age 49 from lung cancer.
Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
